opening.headline: The problem of some being ignored when there are more than 30 rules is solved by reducing the number of instructions and structuring them.
body: Imagine that your customer service assistant's instructions grew one line at a time over the course of a year, reaching 32 lines. Every time a problem arises, I add rules one by one, but at some point, the rules that were previously well followed start to fall out intermittently. The fewer rules you have, the more rules you leave out.

In this lesson, we explore why priorities become blurred as instructions become longer. Next, you will learn how to prioritize rules by grading them, and how to keep the main text in the text and refer to the details for the details. At the end, we unpack together the process of reducing a 30-line manual to five core rules.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Long guidelines can explain why priorities are blurred
Can distinguish between core rules and minor rules

screens.title: With over 30 rules, some are ignored.
screens.lead: First, let's look at what happens in the assistant with longer instructions. Pay attention to which rules are followed and which are left out.

visual.alt: A long list of instructions, with rules followed and rules ignored.

paragraphs: The customer service assistant's instructions increased one line at a time over the course of a year, reaching 32 lines. Refund information rules are generally followed, but greeting format rules are occasionally omitted. Which rules are omitted varies from conversation to conversation, making it difficult to guess the cause.

It may seem like the problem would be solved if there were fewer rules, but the fewer rules there are, the more rules will be missed. Every time a person changes a guideline, it feels like something else is falling apart.
There are two questions in this class. Why do instructions get blurrier as they get longer? And how should we organize it?

screens.outro: First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Do longer instructions lead to better results?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit anything, so think about it first before clicking.

items.prompt: Have you ever added a rule and it ended up doing something that didn't work before?
items.answer: This is a common occurrence. As the number of rules increases, they compete for your Assistant's attention, which can bury some of the existing rules at the expense of new ones. Adding rules isn't always an improvement.

items.prompt: Can you tell which rules are most important just by looking at the instructions?
items.answer: It's hard to tell if there are 30 rows lined up in the same shape. It's difficult to expect an assistant to guess priorities that a human cannot recognize.

items.prompt: If the reader were a new employee, would they know which of the 30 lines to follow first?
items.answer: The golden rule of Claude prompt guidance is this question. If you are confused when you show instructions to a colleague who has little context, there is a good chance that your assistant will be confused as well. Documents that will be confusing to new employees are documents that need to be revised.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by looking at the relationship between instruction length and accuracy.

screens.title: Instruction length and accuracy: It's not the length, it's the clarity of the signal.
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the guideline length. Depending on the length, you can see how clearly the core rules are communicated.

visual.alt: Bar plot showing how key rules become less clear as instruction length increases.
labels: Solution: Break it down and structure it

stops.body: If your rules are ten or so lines long, each one will stand out. There is less competition between rules, and readers can immediately tell which rules are key. Claude It's easy to pass the golden rule of prompt guidance: instructions that aren't confusing when shown to colleagues with little context. At this length, the core rules are usually clearly communicated.

After twenty lines, you start to see competition between the rules. If you have a mix of important and minor rules that look the same, the document can't tell you which comes first. What is needed at this stage is not to write more rules, but to indicate priorities. For each sentence you add, you must ask yourself whether the explanation is necessary or whether it is information you already know.

Beyond thirty lines, it's easy for some rules to get buried. The skill creation instructions say that brevity is key, and explain that every token in the loaded content competes for context with the conversation history. Longer instructions make up less important core rules, so increasing length does not increase accuracy, but rather blurs the signal.

So the solution is not to write more, but to reduce and structure. Erase anything you already know or explanation you only need once. Prioritize the remaining rules, and move detailed procedures and exceptions to references outside the text. This keeps the instructions short but doesn't lose the information you need.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the length issue, let's look at how to indicate priority.

screens.title: Indicate priority: Let the document tell you what comes first
screens.lead: Select each passage highlighted in the example instructions below. A description of how priorities are displayed appears.

data.text:
[Excerpt from Customer Service Guidelines]
## Be sure to keep it
1. Verify your identity first before requesting a refund or account change.
2. Refunds are processed up to 50,000 won per transaction; any amount exceeding this limit is transferred to a customer service representative.
3. If you don’t know the answer, we will guide you through connecting to a counselor without guessing.
## Speech and format
4. Begin the first sentence with a greeting and use respectful language.
5. Responses must not exceed four sentences.
## Situational details
6. For inquiries regarding shipping delays, refer to the shipping inquiry notice document.
7. For exchange inquiries, refer to the exchange procedure document.

marks.note: This is the part where the grade is indicated by the title. GPT guidance tells us to visually distinguish priorities and steps with titles and lists. If you collect the rules that can lead to an accident if broken in the top section, both the assistant and the person will know what comes first.

marks.span: 1. Verify your identity first before requesting a refund or account change.
marks.note: This is a core rule that shows the order by number. If you write a rule with steps in the form of doing this in this situation, the intention becomes clear. Position alone conveys priority without strong emphasis.

marks.span: 3. If you don’t know the answer, we will guide you through connecting to a counselor without guessing.
marks.note: This rule is written in plain sentences without using strong emphasis. Claude's guide says that overuse of intensifiers can lead to overreactions, so it's safer to only use intensifiers in one or two places where they're really needed.

This is a section where grades below the core are divided by title. Dividing sections with delimiters reveals the different nature of the rules, and allows readers to determine which comes first when rules from different sections conflict.

This is the place for minor rules. The content of this section is a candidate for moving into a reference document rather than being left at length in the main text. In the next screen, we'll look at this method of moving, layering.

screens.outro: Once you've indicated your priorities, next is layering, which takes the details out of the text.

screens.title: Layering of rules: main text, details by reference
screens.lead: Select each item to see how tiering works. Pay attention to the boundary between what to keep in the text and what to leave out.

visual.alt: Structure diagram with short text instructions followed by two reference documents that can be opened when needed.

items.answer: The structure is such that the core rules are included in the main text, and detailed procedures and exceptions are excluded as separate materials. Keep the text short and clear, and refer to details only when necessary. Instead of putting everything in one document, divide the document into layers.

items.prompt: How does a Skill document implement this structure?
items.answer: The Skill document describes phased disclosure. Only the name and description are read first, the text is read when skills are needed, and additional files are read when more are needed. We don't put everything in context from the beginning. Additionally, there are instructions to keep the body of SKILL.md within 500 lines.

items.prompt: How do I do this in Project or GPT?
items.answer: Detailed manuals are uploaded as knowledge files, and only one line is written in the instructions telling when to view the material. For example, for inquiries about delivery delays, refer to the delivery tracking information document. The text serves as the standard for judgment, and the file serves as detailed facts.

items.prompt: What do you keep in the text and what do you leave out?
items.answer: The GPT guide also divides rules and actions into guidelines and references into knowledge. Rules that lead to accidents if broken and actions that always apply are included in the text, and details and exceptions that vary depending on the situation, as well as long tables and lists, are sent as reference materials.

screens.outro: Now that you understand the structure, let's solve an example of actually reducing a 30-line manual.

screens.title: Commentary: Reduce 30 lines of customer service manual to 5 key lines
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to follow the instructor as he narrows it down to 30 lines. Pay attention to what you move in each step.

visual.alt: The thirty-line list on the left is divided into three groups and reduced to short instruction boxes on the right.
labels: If you break it, an accident will occur.
Body instructions (5 lines + 2 lines + 1 reference line)

steps.title: Divide the thirty lines into three groups.
steps.body: First, divide the 30 lines into three groups according to your personality: things that will cause accidents if you break them, tone and format of speech, and situational details. If you divide it like this, you can see the weight of the rules mixed in the same shape. For this example, let's say there are nine lines of rules for thinking, seven lines of tone and format, and sixteen lines of situational details.

steps.title: Pick five core rules
steps.body: Pick the five most important things from the bundle of accidents. For example, rules such as verifying personal information, refund limit, and connecting to an agent if you do not know. The remaining four lines are checked to see if they overlap with these five, and if so, they are merged, and if not, they are sent to the context-specific details.

steps.title: Combine tone and form in two lines
steps.body: Speech tone and format The seven lines have a lot of overlap, such as politeness, starting with a greeting, and within four sentences. Combine them into two lines and show the shape with one example. An example conveys the idea more clearly than a lengthy explanation.

steps.title: Move details to knowledge file
steps.body: The 16 lines of detailed information for each situation are moved to the knowledge file, and only one line is left in the instructions indicating that the document should be referred to in case of delivery delay or exchange inquiry. It's not that the details have disappeared, it's just that they've moved to where you need them when you need them.

steps.title: result
steps.body: The text instructions have been reduced to five lines of rules, two lines of format, and one line of references. The importance of core rules increases, reducing the number of rules that are ignored. The refund limit rule, previously one of 32 lines, is now one of five lines and is much more visible.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the reduction process, let's also look at the criteria for judging whether the reduced guidelines are doing their job.

screens.title: Commentary: Criteria for judging whether the reduced guidelines are doing their job
screens.lead: Select each criterion and expand it. A commentary appears explaining how the shortened guidance meets these criteria.

items.title: Criterion 1: Core rules are visible at the top of the list
items.body: The abbreviated guidelines place a must-follow section at the top and list five rules by number. Readers can see the key points on the first screen. If the key is buried in the middle of the list, it doesn't meet this criterion.

items.title: Criterion 2: Does each rule prescribe a different behavior?
items.body: The five rules are identity verification, refund limit, connection if you don't know, greeting and politeness, and only one action each within four sentences. If two rules use the same word differently, combine them or delete one. Each sentence should define one action so they don't conflict with each other.

items.title: Criteria 3: Are there clues in the text to find the translated details?
items.body: In the text, there is a reference line indicating that for inquiries about delivery delay, refer to the delivery tracking information document, and for exchange inquiries, refer to the exchange procedure document. Without a clue, your assistant may not be able to take advantage of the fact that a knowledge file exists.

items.title: Criterion 4: Have failures from the 30-line era disappeared?
items.body: Confirm by reinserting conversations where greetings were missing from the preview and conversations where refund limits were blurred. The guidance on skill creation also emphasizes the need to check and refine through actual use. If the number of failures has not decreased, you need to find out what rules are still buried.

screens.outro: Now that we've checked the standards, let's summarize the key points of this class.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarizes the contents of this class. As you read, try to answer the initial question: Why is it blurry and how do I organize it?

paragraphs: The first question was why the instructions get blurry the longer they get and how to organize them. As the number of rules increases, they compete for attention and some become buried, so the solution is not to write more, but to write less and structure.

Structuring is done in two ways. One is priority marking. Indicate the level through the title and list position, and use emphasis only in one or two places where it is absolutely necessary. The other is stratification. Keep the main points in the main text, send details and exceptions to reference materials such as knowledge files, and leave only clues to find them in the main text.
After reducing, be sure to preview and re-input the previously failed dialogue. Reduction is not something that can be done all at once; it is something that needs to be checked and refined.

Go back to the thirty-two line instructions in the first scene. Now, when you want to add a rule, you are first asked whether this rule is key or detailed, and whether it overlaps with an existing rule. This question is the most practical habit to keep your instructions from getting too long again. The same applies anywhere in ChatGPT's GPT, Claude Project, or Gem.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The structure of instructions is more important than their length. A document that shows what to keep in mind when handed to a new employee is also a clear document for the assistant.

glossary.def: It is about attaching grades and order to rules to reveal what comes first. It is best to indicate this with a title and position in the list.
The structure is to place the core in the main text and the details and exceptions in the reference material.
Like a skill, the name and description are read first, and the text and additional files are loaded only when needed.
If the guidelines become longer, the rules may compete with each other and some may be buried. Length does not equal accuracy.

misconceptions.myth: The fewer the rules, the better they are followed.
misconceptions.fact: As the guidelines become longer, the rules compete with each other and some of them are buried. Before adding rules, try to reduce them and see if you can structure them.

misconceptions.myth: Adding an emphasis to every rule gives it priority.
misconceptions.fact: Overuse of emphatic words can lead to overreactions. Priority is expressed through list position and title, and emphasis is used only where absolutely necessary.

misconceptions.myth: Detailed procedures must also be included in the text of the guidelines.
misconceptions.fact: Leave the details in the knowledge file and leave only clues in the text telling you when to look at the material.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The structure of instructions is more important than their length.
Layer the key points in the main text and the details in reference materials.
Priorities are indicated by location, title, and level, and emphasis is used sparingly.
After reducing, preview to see if previous failures are gone.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What are the five core rules in my guidelines that should not be broken, and where can I move the rest?

checks.q: When I added ‘must’ and ‘absolute’ to every rule in the guidelines, the assistant overreacted. A better way to indicate priorities?
options: Write the emphasized word larger and write the same rule once more.
Emphasis is used only in one or two places where it is absolutely necessary, and the rank is indicated by the list position and title.
Remove all emphasized words and lay out the rules in random order.
Concatenate all rules into one paragraph to form one sentence.
checks.explain: Excessive use of emphasized words can lead to overreactions, so place key rules at the top, separate them with titles, and use emphasized words sparingly.

wrong.0: Increasing repetition and emphasis creates more competition between rules, burying some of them.
wrong.2: If the order is random, the document cannot tell you which comes first.
wrong.3: Combining them into one paragraph loses structure and makes priorities more blurred.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Arrange the 30 lines of the customer service manual in an order that focuses on key rules.
items: The thirty lines are divided into three groups: accident occurrence, tone and form, and situational details.
Pick five key rules from the accident-prone bundle.
Combine tone and format in two lines and show one example.
Move contextual details to a knowledge file and leave a single reference line in the instructions.
checks.explain: First, group by personality, select the key points, combine the format, and remove the details into a knowledge file to make the text shorter and clearer.
checks.intro: Pause for a moment and check your understanding. It will not be submitted or graded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.
